statement: Leadership approves a risk appetite statement, and it is turned into measurable tolerance limits, such as a maximum acceptable downtime or highest acceptable residual rating. The risk response options of accept, mitigate, transfer and avoid are defined, with criteria for choosing among them, including when outsourcing or cloud arrangements are acceptable. All of this is communicated to risk owners and reviewed on a defined cycle. Proof is the approved statement, its version history and distribution records.
why_asked: Without stated limits, risk owners accept or reject risk by personal judgment and leadership cannot tell whether exposure is within what it intended to carry.
how_to_ask: Ask for the appetite statement and look for limits a risk owner could measure against. Then ask how risk owners were told. Example probe: "What is the highest residual risk rating you will accept, who set it, and how does a risk owner know it?"
question: Does your organization have leadership-approved risk appetite and tolerance limits that risk owners use to choose how to respond to risk?
expected_evidence: Approved risk appetite statement; risk tolerance statements with measurable limits; risk response criteria including acceptance and shared-responsibility conditions; distribution or briefing records for risk owners; version history showing the last review
good_looks_like: Leadership has approved an appetite statement. Tolerance limits are measurable. The response options and the criteria for choosing among them are written, including conditions for outsourced and cloud arrangements. Risk owners received the statements and the statements carry a dated review.
test: Obtain the appetite and tolerance statements and the response criteria. Check leadership approval, at least one measurable limit and a review date within the organization's cycle. Sample three risk owners and check each received the statements. Pass if all checks hold.
baseline_risk: Risk is accepted inconsistently and leadership exposure grows beyond what it would knowingly choose.

statement: Cybersecurity and supply chain risks sit in the same enterprise risk process and register as other enterprise risks, and are assessed by a method that covers supplier risk. Written criteria set when a risk is escalated, and defined channels exist for raising it, including risk that starts with suppliers. Risks that meet the threshold are routed through those channels, and enterprise risk reports to leadership include them. Proof is the criteria, an escalation record and the latest leadership report.
why_asked: Security and supplier risks held in a separate list never reach leadership, so they are not weighed against other business risks.
how_to_ask: Ask where cybersecurity and supplier risks are recorded and how one reaches leadership. Ask for a real escalation. Example probe: "Walk me through the last supplier risk that went to senior management and where it appears in the enterprise risk report."
question: Does your organization include cybersecurity and supplier risks in its enterprise risk process, with defined criteria for escalating them to leadership?
expected_evidence: Enterprise risk register extract showing cybersecurity and supplier risks; escalation criteria and channel description; escalation records; latest enterprise risk report to leadership; supplier performance reviews; covering the audit period
good_looks_like: Cybersecurity and supplier risks share one register and method with other risks. Escalation criteria and channels are written and cover third-party risk. At least one risk was escalated through the channel and reached leadership. Supply chain security is part of the wider risk program and is tracked at more than one point in a supplier relationship.
test: Obtain the register, escalation criteria and the latest leadership risk report. Check cybersecurity and supplier risks appear in the register and the report. Sample three risks above the threshold and check each was escalated through the defined channel. Pass if all hold.
baseline_risk: Material security and supplier risks stay below leadership view and are never traded off against other enterprise risks.

statement: Departures from policy are approved through a defined process. Each exception needs a recorded approval and an expiry or review date. An exception register holds an owner and a review date for each open exception, each exception is tracked to closure, and policy violations are recorded with how each was handled. Proof is the register, approval records and violation records.
why_asked: Open-ended waivers turn into permanent unmanaged risk, and nobody can show which departures from policy were approved or why.
how_to_ask: Ask for the exception register and look for open items without an owner or date. Ask what happens when an exception expires. Example probe: "Show me an exception that expired in the last year. Who reviewed it and what was decided?"
question: Does your organization approve departures from policy through a defined process that sets an expiry or review date for each?
expected_evidence: Exception procedure; exception register with owners, approvals and review dates; records of policy violations and how each was handled; covering the audit period
good_looks_like: Every exception has a recorded approval, an owner and an expiry or review date. Expired exceptions are closed or re-approved. Violations are recorded with the action taken. Departures that touch change management are assessed for their security impact first.
test: Obtain the exception register for the period. Sample five open and closed exceptions and check each has approval, an owner and an expiry or review date. Sample any violations and check the handling is recorded. Pass if no sampled exception is open-ended and all handling is recorded.
baseline_risk: Policy waivers accumulate with no owner or end date, so known weaknesses persist and cannot be defended to an auditor.

statement: The risk method requires internal and external threats, including insiders, to be identified. Identified threats are recorded in a threat register, or in the risk register, and the entries are updated from threat intelligence on a defined cycle. Proof is the method, the register and its version history.
why_asked: Risk ratings built on an outdated or incomplete threat picture understate exposure to the attacks actually in play.
how_to_ask: Ask for the threat register and how it is updated. Look for insider threats and recent changes. Example probe: "Which threats were added or changed after your last threat intelligence review, and where did that information come from?"
question: Does your organization keep a current register of internal and external threats, including insiders?
expected_evidence: Risk assessment method requiring threat identification; threat register or risk register with internal, insider and external threats; version history showing updates from threat intelligence; covering the audit period
good_looks_like: The method requires threats to be identified. The register lists internal, insider and external threats. Entries were updated in the period from named intelligence sources.
test: Obtain the method, the register and its version history. Check the method requires threat identification and the register lists internal and external threats including insiders. Sample three entries and check at least one update in the period cites threat intelligence. Pass if all hold.
baseline_risk: New attack methods go unrecognized, so risk assessments miss the threats most likely to occur.
